passages.text: <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variant-specific synaptic dysfunction is associated with network hyperexcitability in human iPSC-derived neurons
Summary
Background

Variants in <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic>/syntaxin-1B are linked to a spectrum of fever-associated epilepsy syndromes. <sentence_start/>While studies in murine models have provided mechanistic insights, their relevance to human disease in a heterozygous context may be limited.
Methods

We investigated two pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants using isolated single neurons and neuronal network cultures derived from patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells. <sentence_start/>These carried either a <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> p.G226R variant, associated with severe developmental epilepsy, or an InDel variant (p.K45delinsRCMIE/p.L46M) linked to a transient familial seizure syndrome. <sentence_start/>Synaptic function and network excitability were assessed using patch-clamp and multi-electrode array recordings, alongside morphological and transcriptomic profiling.
Findings

G226R exhibited both gain- and loss-of-function characteristics, with increased miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency in networks but not in autapses, and synaptic failure during sustained high-frequency stimulation. <sentence_start/>For the InDel variant, the predicted loss-of-function phenotype based on reduced syntaxin-1B levels was not detectable at the single-cell level, likely masked by compensatory synaptic upregulation. <sentence_start/>At the network level, however, both variants were associated with neuronal hyperexcitability, characterised by more frequent and prolonged bursting activity, with a much stronger phenotype in G226R-containing networks. <sentence_start/>Transcriptomic profiling revealed a differential dysregulation of synaptic and other neuronal genes.
Interpretation

The divergence between morphological, electrophysiological and transcriptomic findings suggests that compensatory mechanisms may contribute to network hyperexcitability. <sentence_start/>Initially engaged to maintain homoeostasis, they may ultimately contribute to a pathological network state. <sentence_start/>The graded severity of network alterations across <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants correlates with the clinical phenotypes.

Research in context
Evidence before this study

Heterozygous variants in the <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> gene have been associated with a wide range of epilepsy syndromes, but their functional consequences remain unclear. <sentence_start/>Previous studies using mouse neurons identified variant-specific effects only in a <italic toggle="yes">Stx1a/Stx1b</italic> double knockout background, a condition with limited relevance to human physiology, whereas functional effects were absent in a heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic> background.
Added value of this study

We examined two paradigmatic <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants in a human model using patient-derived iPSC neurons. <sentence_start/>By integrating single-cell electrophysiology, network-level recordings, and molecular profiling, we uncovered distinct forms of synaptic dysfunction, covering both gain- and loss-of-function effects, that converge on a shared, but graded, network-level hyperactivity phenotype. <sentence_start/>The human iPSC model captured functional consequences not evident in heterozygous mouse systems, offering mechanistic insight into how <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants are associated with pathological network activity in epilepsy.
Implications of all the available evidence

This study underscores the value of patient-specific models in unravelling the pathomechanisms of human neurological disorders. <sentence_start/>In addition, the inherent limitations of <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic> systems highlight the need for more advanced models that capture synaptic heterogeneity and cell-type-specific features to more precisely characterise synaptic dysfunction. <sentence_start/>Taken together, these approaches will help to further elucidate the exact mechanisms of <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic>-related pathology and enable the rational development of future treatment strategies.
Introduction

Neuronal communication relies on the conversion of electrical signals into chemical ones, facilitated by the controlled release of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles at presynaptic sites. <sentence_start/>This release is primarily mediated by the three neuronal N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins: syntaxin-1, synaptobrevin, and SNAP-25.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-biophys-111821-104732" pmid="35167762" pmcid="PMC9490555" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The assembly of this core SNARE complex drives the fusion of the vesicle membrane with the presynaptic membrane, releasing enough energy to overcome the energetic barrier of fusing two negatively charged phospholipid bilayers.<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnmol.2021.733138" pmcid="PMC8377282" pmid="34421538" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bpj.2022.07.013" pmid="35810329" pmcid="PMC9463651" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation>

Through its interactions with other SNARE-associated proteins, syntaxin-1 emerges as a key player in regulating the fusion process.<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/emboj/18.16.4372" pmid="10449403" pmcid="PMC1171512" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10858-008-9239-1" pmid="18458823" pmcid="PMC2685195" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/22768" pmid="10440375" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1230473" pmid="23258414" pmcid="PMC3733786" count="1">7</citation> This regulatory function is driven by the presence of a distinctive N-terminal H<sub>abc</sub>-domain, which is structurally complemented by the SNARE-specific subdomain that is essential for the complex assembly.<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/2211-5463.13473" pmcid="PMC9623538" pmid="35986639" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/emboj.2012.307" pmid="23188083" pmcid="PMC3545302" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The significance of these two subdomains is also highlighted by their conservation among the two neuronal isoforms, syntaxin-1a and syntaxin-1b, which exhibit 84% homology in their amino acid sequences.<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1321498" pmid="1321498" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This structural similarity suggests partial functional redundancy. <sentence_start/>Indeed, while knockout of one of the two other SNARE proteins, synaptobrevin and SNAP-25, results in a marked reduction in evoked synaptic transmission,<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1064335" pmid="11691998" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nn783" pmid="11753414" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> <italic toggle="yes">Stx1a</italic><sup>−/−</sup> mice develop normally and show no major effect on fast synaptic transmission.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0289-06.2006" pmid="16723534" pmcid="PMC6675267" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In contrast, <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic><sup>−/−</sup> mice die shortly after birth and exhibit synaptic defects such as a reduced frequency of miniature postsynaptic currents, highlighting the distinct and more critical role of <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic> in maintaining basal synaptic function.<citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0090004" pmcid="PMC3938564" pmid="24587181" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1314-16.2016" pmid="27466336" pmcid="PMC6601879" count="1">15</citation>, <citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jn.00577.2015" pmid="26203110" pmcid="PMC4620129" count="1">16</citation>

The importance of the human <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> gene was further highlighted in a study by our group, which associated variants in <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> with a wide spectrum of genetic epilepsy syndromes.<citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3130" pmid="25362483" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Since then, <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic>-associated epilepsies form a distinct subgroup within the broader category of disorders related to synaptic dysfunction, collectively known as synaptopathies.<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2020.05.036" pmid="32559416" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The pathogenic variants in <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> extend across the entire protein structure, but cluster particularly in the regulatory H<sub>abc</sub>-domain as well as the SNARE motif.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000007089" pmid="30737342" pmcid="PMC6511102" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic>-related synaptopathies present with clinical manifestations that vary in severity from mild genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) to severe forms of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), with the latter exhibiting severe seizures and concurrent developmental delay or regression.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000007089" pmid="30737342" pmcid="PMC6511102" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The causal pathogenic variants are equally diverse and encompass missense or truncating variants as well as partial or even whole gene deletions. <sentence_start/>Our group could show that protein truncating variants were mostly associated with milder syndromes, whereas missense variants particularly in the SNARE motif caused more often severe encephalopathies.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000007089" pmid="30737342" pmcid="PMC6511102" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Even though all these variants affect the function of the same protein, this variant diversity appears to give rise to various synaptic dysfunctions, ultimately matching the clinical heterogeneity.

In an attempt to observe the proposed diversity of synaptic malfunctions at the molecular level, a previous study by Vardar et al. investigated three paradigmatic <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants V216E, G226R, and InDel (p.K45delinsRCMIE and p.L46M) using patch-clamp electrophysiology on mouse autaptic cultures, and biochemical and structural approaches.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awaa151" pmid="32572454" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This led to the identification of distinct synaptic dysfunctions for all three variants when expressed on a <italic toggle="yes">Stx1a/Stx1b</italic> double knockout background. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the InDel variant resulted in an unfolded syntaxin-1B protein that completely failed to sustain neurotransmission, whereas G226R displayed partial loss-of-function (LOF) characteristics. <sentence_start/>V216E, in contrast, displayed gain-of-function (GOF) features, evident as an increased release probability of synaptic vesicles. <sentence_start/>Notably, the synaptic malfunctions were mostly absent in a heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic><sup>+/−</sup> background. <sentence_start/>As this approach aimed to more closely mimic the heterozygous patient situation, the translatability of the synaptic phenotypes in a double knockout condition in mice remains under debate.

To overcome this limitation, we investigated two of these pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants in a human-relevant context. <sentence_start/>We used patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons carrying either the aforementioned G226R missense variant or the complex InDel variant. <sentence_start/>While the investigation at the single-cell autaptic level allowed an in-depth analysis of synaptic electrophysiology, the concurrent analysis using multi-electrode arrays (MEAs) demonstrated the network consequences of the synaptic dysfunction. <sentence_start/>Finally, morphological and transcriptomic analyses further suggested the involvement of secondary mechanisms that may connect the primary synaptic deficits to the observed hyperexcitable network state. <sentence_start/>Understanding both the phenotypic diversity and the shared features among <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic>-related synaptopathies is crucial for advancing the development of potentially tailored therapeutic strategies.
Methods
Generation and validation of iPSC lines

The two carriers of the InDel variant were both female and related (mother and daughter). <sentence_start/>Both individuals were diagnosed with GEFS+ and are currently seizure-free without medication. <sentence_start/>Skin biopsies were obtained in October 2016, at the ages of 36 and 56 years, respectively. <sentence_start/>The patient carrying the G226R variant was also female, and the skin biopsy was collected in May 2020, at the age of 14 years. <sentence_start/>This patient was diagnosed with DEE and is under seizure control with levetiracetam, stiripentol, and valproate. <sentence_start/>The two control individuals were unrelated, healthy, non-commercial donors. <sentence_start/>iPSCs from Control 1 were derived from skin fibroblasts obtained from foreskin tissue collected during a circumcision in February 2013 at the age of 6 years from a male donor, while cells from Control 2 were derived from keratinocytes isolated from a hair root of a female donor in October 2014 at the age of 30 years. <sentence_start/>All donors were of Caucasian ancestry. <sentence_start/>The two control lines were reprogrammed in 2013 and 2014 and were maintained as cryopreserved iPSCs until use, whereas all patient-derived lines were reprogrammed in 2020. <sentence_start/>Patient-derived fibroblasts carrying the InDel variant were reprogrammed using a retroviral-based method with pMXs vectors encoding the four Yamanaka factors OCT3/4 (#17217, Addgene), SOX2 (#17218, Addgene), KLF4 (#17219, Addgene) and c-MYC (#17220, Addgene). <sentence_start/>All vectors were gifts from Shinya Yamanaka. <sentence_start/>Details on the viral reprogramming process are described in Haag et al.<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scr.2023.103028" pmid="36652844" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Fibroblasts derived from the patient carrying the p.G226R variant were reprogrammed using the non-integrative ReproRNA™-OKSGM Kit (5930, Stemcell Technologies), following the manufacturer's instructions. <sentence_start/>Emerging iPSC colonies were manually selected and cultured on Matrigel-coated (354277, Corning) plates in mTeSR medium (85850, Stemcell Technologies). <sentence_start/>Two iPSC clones were generated per patient. <sentence_start/>For the G226R variant, both clones were used in downstream experiments, while for the InDel variant, one clone per patient was selected for further analyses. <sentence_start/>Following reprogramming, all generated iPSC clones underwent karyotyping at the Institute of Medical Genetics and Applied Genomics in Tübingen to confirm the absence of major chromosomal abnormalities. <sentence_start/>The presence of the respective pathogenic variants was confirmed by PCR and subsequent Sanger sequencing (LGC Genomics) using variant-specific primers (G226R forward: 5′-TTGTAGCTCTCTCCCTCGTCA-3′, G226R reverse: 5′-AGATCGACACACGGACAGAT-3′; InDel forward: 5′-TGCTCATGGACTCAGCCTTC-3′, InDel reverse: 5′-GTGAGATGTCTGGGTGGGAAC-3′). <sentence_start/>For this purpose, genomic DNA was extracted using the QuickExtract™ DNA Extraction Solution (QE0905T, LGC Biosearch Technologies). <sentence_start/>To ensure mycoplasma-free cultures, routine screening was performed using the TaKaRa PCR Mycoplasma Detection Set (6601, TaKaRa Bio) according to the manufacturer's instructions. <sentence_start/>Finally, pluripotency of the iPSC clones was confirmed by RT-qPCR using the SensiFAST SYBR Lo-Rox One-Step Kit (74001, Bioline) and the ISOLATE II RNA Mini Kit (52072, Bioline) for RNA extraction, as well as by immunocytochemistry employing established pluripotency markers. <sentence_start/>Details on antibodies and their respective dilutions are provided in the Immunocytochemistry methods section. <sentence_start/>The RT-qPCR primers used for viral and RNA-based reprogramming are detailed in Haag et al.<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scr.2023.103028" pmid="36652844" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> and Murti et al.,<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scr.2020.102137" pmid="33418202" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> respectively.
Site-specific integration of <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic> into the AAVS1 locus

Stable iPSC lines with inducible Neurogenin-2 (<italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>) expression were generated using a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated approach targeting the <italic toggle="yes">AAVS1</italic> safe-harbour locus. <sentence_start/>The pXAT2 plasmid (#80494, Addgene) encoded the Cas9 enzyme and an AAVS1-specific single guide RNA, while the pUCM-AAVS1-TO-hNGN2 plasmid (#105840, Addgene) carried a doxycycline-inducible <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic> transgene, the reverse tetracycline transactivator (rtTA), and a puromycin resistance cassette, all flanked by <italic toggle="yes">AAVS1</italic> homology arms. <sentence_start/>Both plasmids were kindly provided by Knut Woltjen and Michael Ward, respectively. <sentence_start/>iPSCs were nucleofected with 1 μg of each plasmid using the Nucleofector™ Transfection 2 b Device (Lonza) and the Human Stem Cell Nucleofector™ Kit 2 (Lonza), following the manufacturer's instructions. <sentence_start/>Cells were then plated onto Matrigel-coated wells in mTeSR medium supplemented with 10 μM Y-27632 (1254, Tocris) to promote survival. <sentence_start/>Puromycin (ant-pr-1, InvivoGen) selection (0.5 μg/mL for 72 h) was initiated after colony emergence to enrich for stably integrated clones. <sentence_start/>Positively selected lines were expanded, cryopreserved, and used for downstream applications.
<italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-based network culture differentiation

iPSCs were maintained in mTeSR medium with daily medium changes until neuronal induction. <sentence_start/>On the induction day, cells were pre-treated with 2.5 μg/mL doxycycline (D9891, Sigma-Aldrich) for 5 h to initiate <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic> expression, and 10 μM Y-27632 was added 1 h prior to dissociation to enhance cell survival.<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2013.05.029" pmid="23764284" pmcid="PMC3751803" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/msb.20145508" pmid="25403753" pmcid="PMC4299601" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> Following enzymatic detachment with accutase (A6964, Sigma-Aldrich), the cells were resuspended in neural stem cell medium (NSCM; 47.5% Neurobasal Medium (21103049, Gibco), 47.5% DMEM/F12 (21331-020, Gibco), 1% N2 supplement (N2-K, Capricorn), 2% NSC supplement (C21-H, Capricorn), 1% GlutaMAX (35050087, Gibco), 1% non-essential amino acids (P08-32100, PAN-Biotech GmbH), and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin (15140122, Gibco) supplemented with 10 μM Y-27632, 3 μM DAPT (2634, Tocris), and 1 μg/mL doxycycline. <sentence_start/>The cells were then seeded at a density of 60 × 10<sup>3</sup> per coverslip and 40 × 10<sup>3</sup> per well of a 24-well MEA plate (24W700/100F-288, Multi Channel Systems). <sentence_start/>The following day, the medium was replaced with NSCM containing 10 μM DAPT, 10 μM PD0325901 (4192, Tocris), and 1 μg/mL doxycycline. <sentence_start/>From day 5 onward, differentiation was continued in NSCM without additional supplements, with medium changes twice per week. <sentence_start/>To eliminate proliferative precursor cells or incompletely converted iPSCs, the cells were additionally treated with 2 μM cytosine-β-D-arabinofuranoside (Ara-C; C1768, Sigma-Aldrich) from day 8 to day 11. <sentence_start/>For all electrophysiological experiments, <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-induced neurons (iNs) were co-cultured with primary mouse astrocytes, which were plated three days prior to induction at a density of 40 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells per well. <sentence_start/>For immunostaining experiments of iN networks, iNs were cultured on poly-L-ornithine- (P3655, Sigma-Aldrich) and laminin-coated (L2020, Sigma-Aldrich) coverslips.
<italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-induced autaptic neuron generation

Autaptic cultures were generated by seeding iPSC-derived neurons at low density onto astrocyte-covered microislands. <sentence_start/>Microislands were prepared following established protocols by applying discrete dots of a coating solution onto agarose-coated 18 mm coverslips using a custom-built stamping tool.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2019.04.058" pmid="31091456" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-41259-1" pmid="30894602" pmcid="PMC6427022" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2019.04.059" pmid="31091457" count="1">27</citation> The coating solution consisted of 0.5 mg/mL poly-D-lysine (P6407, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 mg/mL collagen (C5533, Sigma-Aldrich), and 17 mM acetic acid (6755.1, Carl Roth GmbH + Co. KG) (1:1:3 ratio). <sentence_start/>Primary mouse astrocytes were plated at a density of 20 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells/well in DMEM (41965039, Gibco) + 10% FBS (P30-3306, PAN-Biotech GmbH). <sentence_start/>Upon confluency, astrocyte microisland cultures were treated with 2 μM Ara-C for at least 24 h. <sentence_start/>For induction, iPSCs were treated with 10 μM Y-27632 for 1 h, washed with PBS (14190094, Gibco), and detached using accutase. <sentence_start/>After centrifugation, the cell pellet was resuspended in NSCM supplemented with 10 μM Y-27632 and 2 μg/mL doxycycline and plated on Matrigel-coated 6-well plates at 300 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells/well. <sentence_start/>The medium was refreshed over the following two days with NSCM + doxycycline (2 μg/mL). <sentence_start/>On day 4, 2 μM Ara-C was added for 24 h. <sentence_start/>On day 5, iNs were harvested and cryopreserved in knockout serum replacement (10828028, Gibco) containing 10% DMSO (A3672, PanReac AppliChem). <sentence_start/>Freshly thawed iNs were plated onto confluent astrocyte microislands at a density of 5-7 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells/well in NSCM supplemented with 10 ng/mL BDNF (450-02, PeproTech), CNTF (450-02, PeproTech), GDNF (450-10, PeproTech), and 0.5% FBS. <sentence_start/>Medium was changed weekly.
Immunocytochemistry

For immunocytochemical stainings, cells were washed with PBS and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 10 min at room temperature (RT). <sentence_start/>After fixation, cells were again washed with PBS and stored at 4 °C. <sentence_start/>To block non-specific binding, coverslips were incubated for 1 h at RT in blocking solution containing 0.2% Triton X-100 (9036-19-5, Sigma-Aldrich) and 10% normal goat serum (NGS; 566380, Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS. <sentence_start/>Cells were then washed and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. <sentence_start/>The next day, secondary antibodies were applied for 1 h at RT in the dark. <sentence_start/>Coverslips were mounted using DAPI Fluoromount-G (0100-20, Southern Biotech). <sentence_start/>All antibodies were diluted in a 1:10 solution of blocking buffer in PBS.

Pluripotency was confirmed using rabbit anti-OCT4 (1:2000; ab19857, Abcam, RRID: ), rabbit anti-SOX2 (1:2000; ab97959, Abcam, RRID: ), mouse anti-SSEA4 (1:2000; ab16287, Abcam, RRID: ), and mouse anti-TRA-1-60 (1:2000; ab16288, Abcam, RRID: ) primary antibodies.
Synapse quantification was performed using rabbit anti-Synapsin (1:1000; ab1543, Sigma-Aldrich, RRID: ) in combination with chicken anti-MAP2 (1:2000; ab5392, Abcam, RRID: ).

For Bassoon-Homer colocalisation stainings, the protocol was modified as follows: Tris-buffered saline (TBS; 150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.6) containing 0.1% Triton X-100 (TBS-Tx) was used instead of PBS throughout the procedure. <sentence_start/>Non-specific binding was blocked with 5% NGS in TBS-Tx. <sentence_start/>Primary antibodies were diluted in blocking solution and included rabbit anti-Homer1 (1:500; Synaptic Systems, 160003, RRID: ) and mouse anti-Bassoon (1:500; Enzo Life Sciences, ADI-VAM-PS003-F, RRID: ), together with chicken anti-MAP2 (1:2000; ab5392, Abcam, RRID: ).
All secondary antibodies were used at a 1:1000 dilution (A-11001, RRID: ; A-11011, RRID: ; A-11039, RRID: ; A-11008, RRID: ; A32731TR, RRID: ; A-11004, RRID: ; A-21449, RRID: , Thermo Fisher).

Images of pluripotency markers were acquired on a Zeiss Axio Imager Apotome 2 fluorescence microscope (Carl Zeiss AG). <sentence_start/>Synapse quantification in autaptic and network cultures was performed using images acquired with a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems) using tile scan and z-stack modes. <sentence_start/>Z-stacks were converted to maximum intensity projections in ImageJ 1.54 (National Institutes of Health) before analysis. <sentence_start/>An automated analysis pipeline was created with CellProfiler 4.2.6. (Broad Institute). <sentence_start/>Soma and neurite regions were defined based on MAP2 signal using adaptive thresholding. <sentence_start/>Synapses were identified by thresholding the synapsin signal and applying a size filter to detect puncta. <sentence_start/>The same analysis pipeline was used for the detection of functional synapses based on Bassoon/Homer colocalisation. <sentence_start/>A MAP2-based neuronal mask ensured synapse quantification was limited to neuronal areas. <sentence_start/>In addition, neurite length was quantified to calculate synaptic density, expressed as synapsin or Bassoon/Homer puncta per 100 μm of neurite length.
Western blot

For protein identification, 5 μg of total cell lysate per lane was loaded onto an 8% SDS-polyacrylamide gel. <sentence_start/>Following electrophoretic separation and transfer, Protran® Nitrocellulose Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk powder and subsequently incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: rabbit anti-<italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> (1:3000, 110403, Synaptic Systems, RRID: ), chicken anti-MAP2 (1:10,000, ab5392, Abcam, RRID: ), or mouse anti-Vinculin (1:2000, V9131, Sigma-Aldrich, RRID: ), all diluted in 5% skim milk in PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20. <sentence_start/>After washing, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies: goat anti-rabbit (Bio-Rad 1706515, RRID: ), goat anti-chicken (Promega G135A, RRID: ), or goat anti-mouse (Bio-Rad 172-1011, RRID: ), each diluted 1:10,000. <sentence_start/>Blots were developed using the Mini-PROTEAN® Tetra Cell according to the manufacturer's instructions. <sentence_start/>Signal quantification was performed using ImageJ. Syntaxin-1B expression levels were normalised to corresponding MAP2 signals in total lysates, and data were pooled from independent experiments.
Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of iPSC-derived neurons

Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed at RT using an Axopatch 200 B amplifier (Molecular Devices), with Clampex 10.2 software (Molecular Devices) controlling data acquisition. <sentence_start/>Recording pipettes were pulled from borosilicate glass and had resistances between 2.5 and 4 MΩ. <sentence_start/>The intracellular solution contained 140 mM K-gluconate, 1 mM CaCl<sub>2</sub>, 10 mM EGTA, 2 mM MgCl<sub>2</sub>, 4 mM Na<sub>2</sub>ATP, and 10 mM HEPES (pH = 7.2, 305 mOsm), while the extracellular artificial cerebrospinal fluid consisted of 140 mM NaCl, 4.2 mM KCl, 1.1 mM CaCl<sub>2</sub>.2H<sub>2</sub>O, 1 mM MgSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O, 0.5 mM Na<sub>2</sub>HPO<sub>4</sub>, 0.45 mM NaH<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, 5 mM HEPES, and 10 mM D-glucose (pH = 7.4, 300 mOsm). <sentence_start/>Series resistance was compensated by 80%, and only cells with access resistances below 12 MΩ were included in the analysis. <sentence_start/>Signals were sampled at 10 kHz and filtered using a 2 kHz low-pass Bessel filter. <sentence_start/>Data analysis was carried out using custom-written routines in MATLAB R2023b (MathWorks).<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) were quantified with the Mini Analysis Program V.6.0.7 (Synaptosoft Inc.). <sentence_start/>In autaptic cultures, iNs were held at a membrane potential of −70 mV, and synaptic responses were triggered by 2 ms depolarisation steps to 0 mV. The present study functionally characterised <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants in a human iPSC-based neuronal system derived from patient-specific cells. <sentence_start/>Prior work in mouse neurons demonstrated that these variants can disrupt synaptic function under an unphysiological condition lacking both <italic toggle="yes">Stx1a</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic>.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awaa151" pmid="32572454" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In this previous model, InDel-expressing neurons represented a complete LOF due to reduced protein stability, while G226R displayed a milder LOF effect on Ca<sup>2+</sup>-triggered neurotransmitter release. <sentence_start/>However, since neither of the two variants exhibited a phenotype in the presence of wild-type syntaxin-1B and syntaxin-1A, their impact on synaptic function in a heterozygous state remains to be determined. <sentence_start/>Addressing this gap, this study investigated the variant effects in a human genetic context, enabling the analysis of disease-relevant mechanisms under conditions that more closely resemble those in affected individuals.

Building on this human model, our electrophysiological analyses revealed that both <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants under investigation were associated with a hyperexcitable network state in <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-induced excitatory neuronal cultures. <sentence_start/>Using MEA recordings, we observed significantly increased burst frequency and length in iN networks derived from affected individuals compared to those from controls, suggesting a shared network-level phenotype despite the distinct molecular nature of the variants. <sentence_start/>Notably, this hyperactivity was significantly more pronounced in G226R-iN networks, aligning with the variants’ association with more severe clinical manifestations. <sentence_start/>Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings further demonstrated that only G226R produced a measurable electrophysiological phenotype at the synaptic level. <sentence_start/>Specifically, G226R showed an increased mEPSC frequency as a network-specific phenotype, along with a failure to maintain neurotransmission during sustained high-frequency activity. <sentence_start/>Importantly, passive and active membrane properties in iN networks were largely unchanged across variants, arguing against cell-autonomous alterations as the basis of the network phenotype. <sentence_start/>Although an increased AHP was observed in InDel neurons, this isolated effect does not readily explain the observed network hyperexcitability, suggesting a predominantly synaptic origin.

in diminished charge transfer and reduced synaptic fidelity during ongoing activity.

In addition to this activity-dependent synaptic fatigue, G226R-iNs exhibited a significantly increased frequency of mEPSCs. <sentence_start/>One plausible mechanism underlying this gain-of-function phenotype is interference of the variant with the clamping activity of synaptotagmin-1. <sentence_start/>Under basal conditions, the SNARE complex must be tightly regulated to prevent premature fusion, with synaptotagmin-1 acting as a calcium-sensitive clamp that stabilises vesicles in a release-ready yet restrained state.<citation rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-019-10391-x" pmid="31160571" pmcid="PMC6546687" count="1"><sup>46</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0092-8674(93)90733-7" pmid="8104705" count="1"><sup>47</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This clamp is based on electrostatic interactions between basic residues of synaptotagmin-1 (R281, K288, R398, R399) and acidic residues on syntaxin-1B (D230, E233, E237) and SNAP25 (D51, E52, E55) (Supplementary Fig. S5b).<citation rid="bib48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature14975" pmid="26280336" pmcid="PMC4607316" count="1"><sup>48</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The G226 residue lies in close proximity to this interface, and its substitution with a bulky, positively charged arginine may alter the local electrostatic environment, potentially weakening synaptotagmin-1 binding. <sentence_start/>Such a disruption has the potential to destabilise the clamped intermediate state and increase the likelihood of spontaneous vesicle fusion.<citation rid="bib49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2409636121" pmcid="PMC11494337" pmid="39374398" count="1"><sup>49</sup></citation>

Of note, the increased frequency of mEPSCs in G226R was observed in iN-as well as mouse-network cultures but not in autaptic cultures. <sentence_start/>This divergence between network and autaptic cultures exemplifies a well-known phenomenon where synaptic phenotypes are often subtle or absent in isolated single neurons yet become apparent within the more physiologically relevant context of interconnected networks.<citation rid="bib50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1341-09.2009" pmid="19515907" pmcid="PMC2723061" count="1">50</citation>, <citation rid="bib51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0062414" pmcid="PMC3639172" pmid="23658626" count="1">51</citation>, <citation rid="bib52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bpsgos.2023.05.004" pmid="38298782" pmcid="PMC10829628" count="1">52</citation> <sentence_start/>Although the exact reasons remain unclear, it is generally thought that the complex synaptic connectivity and interactions present in networks are essential for unmasking these functional alterations.

In contrast to G226R, the complex InDel variant is located within the first helix of the H<sub>abc</sub>-domain.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000007089" pmid="30737342" pmcid="PMC6511102" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The iPSC lines used in this study were derived from two related individuals with GEFS + who experienced a mild form of epilepsy that resolved during childhood without further treatment. <sentence_start/>This clinical presentation aligns with the network-level hyperactivity observed in InDel-derived cultures, which, however, did not translate into detectable synaptic alterations at the single-cell level.

Structurally, the deletion of K45 combined with the insertion of five additional amino acids and the L46M substitution disrupts syntaxin-1B protein stability and leads to a non-functional protein in autapses of <italic toggle="yes">Stx1a</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic> knock-out mice.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awaa151" pmid="32572454" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In line with these results, protein quantification by Western blot showed reduced levels of syntaxin-1B in InDel-iNs. <sentence_start/>Prior studies in <italic toggle="yes">Stx1b</italic> knockout mice reported a smaller RRP size, decreased vesicular release probability, and reduced mEPSC frequency.<citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0090004" pmcid="PMC3938564" pmid="24587181" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1314-16.2016" pmid="27466336" pmcid="PMC6601879" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0187-13.2013" pmid="24133272" pmcid="PMC6618535" count="1"><sup>53</sup></citation> These findings are indicative of a LOF phenotype that would be anticipated in the context of reduced syntaxin-1B protein. <sentence_start/>In the present study, however, InDel-iNs did not show comparable deficits in single-cell electrophysiology. <sentence_start/>Instead, synaptic density was markedly increased, reaching more than twice the level of controls, while the strength of synaptic responses remained unchanged. <sentence_start/>Given the established inverse relationship between synapse number and release probability,<citation rid="bib54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2008.07.006" pmid="18701072" pmcid="PMC6390949" count="1"><sup>54</sup></citation> this likely reflects a homoeostatic adjustment to compensate for impaired release efficiency and may effectively mask the expected LOF phenotype.

The higher synaptic density observed in InDel-iNs additionally corresponds with changes in the expression of genes related to cytoskeletal dynamics and neuronal morphology. <sentence_start/>Notably, these neurons also show a strong upregulation of the SNARE protein SNAP25. <sentence_start/>While SNAP25 cannot simply replace the function of syntaxin-1B,<citation rid="bib55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0896-6273(00)81177-0" pmid="10839363" count="1"><sup>55</sup></citation> its elevated expression may enhance the binding efficiency of the remaining syntaxin-1B protein. <sentence_start/>The syntaxin-1-SNAP25 dimer is a critical and rate-limiting intermediate in SNARE assembly<citation rid="bib56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-68476-3" pmcid="PMC7363831" pmid="32669573" count="1"><sup>56</sup></citation> and also supports neuronal survival independently of neurotransmission.<citation rid="bib57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms2462" pmid="23403573" pmcid="PMC4052923" count="1"><sup>57</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Therefore, elevated levels of SNAP25 could increase the probability of effective interactions with residual wild-type syntaxin-1B, helping to preserve synaptic output in isolated neurons while promoting aberrant network-level excitability.

Although neurons containing either InDel or G226R share a remarkable overlap in synapse-related differentially expressed genes, G226R-iNs also exhibit distinct transcriptional changes. <sentence_start/>The upregulation of <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> in G226R-iNs, despite normal protein abundance, may reflect increased protein turnover driven by the gain-of-function phenotype: elevated spontaneous vesicle fusion increases SNARE complex consumption, while the reduced Munc18-1 interaction may render syntaxin-1B more susceptible to degradation in its unbound state, collectively necessitating higher transcriptional output to maintain steady-state protein levels. <sentence_start/>Notably, although InDel-iNs present with reduced syntaxin-1B protein (a condition that would equally warrant transcriptional upregulation), these neurons appear to engage alternative compensatory mechanisms, including increased synaptic density and <italic toggle="yes">SNAP25</italic> upregulation, rather than elevating <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> expression itself. <sentence_start/>Additionally, downregulation of <italic toggle="yes">RIMBP2</italic>, a key active zone organiser involved in vesicle tethering and replenishment,<citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2020.107960" pmid="32755572" count="1"><sup>58</sup></citation> may correlate with the impairment in synaptic reliability. <sentence_start/>Concomitant dysregulation of RAB-associated genes suggests broader disruption of vesicle trafficking and recycling pathways.<citation rid="bib59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/21541248.2016.1277001" pmid="28146371" pmcid="PMC5902211" count="1"><sup>59</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The observed downregulation of DLG4 (PSD-95), together with upregulation of DLG2 and reduced expression of the AMPA receptor auxiliary subunit SHISA6, points towards postsynaptic remodelling with potentially altered receptor stabilisation and synaptic organisation. <sentence_start/>Notably, SHISA6 has been shown to prevent synaptically trapped AMPARs from depression during high-frequency synaptic transmission,<citation rid="bib60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms10682" pmcid="PMC4778035" pmid="26931375" count="1"><sup>60</sup></citation> suggesting that its reduced expression may further compromise postsynaptic responsiveness under sustained activity. <sentence_start/>Together, these changes may represent a molecular correlate of the mixed loss- and gain-of-function phenotype, characterised by increased spontaneous excitatory activity in networks but impaired synaptic reliability during sustained high-frequency stimulation.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the increased network activity observed in InDel and G226R neurons may arise from partially convergent, compensatory mechanisms that are initially triggered by distinct primary synaptic dysfunctions. <sentence_start/>G226R appears to affect synaptic transmission through LOF mechanisms, such as synaptic failure during sustained high-frequency activity, and GOF effects, including enhanced spontaneous vesicle release. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the InDel variant primarily reduces syntaxin-1B protein levels, reflecting a classical LOF phenotype. <sentence_start/>In both cases, transcriptomic adaptations engage homoeostatic mechanisms aimed at stabilising synaptic function, yet these compensatory changes may paradoxically increase susceptibility to network hyperexcitability and contribute to disease-relevant neuronal phenotypes.

It is important to consider that the described compensatory mechanisms were observed in a purely excitatory <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-derived neuronal network, which not only lacks inhibitory neurons but also the broader cell-type diversity found <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>Therefore, this setup likely triggers strong homoeostatic responses that may not accurately represent the complex dynamics of the human brain. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the model does not reflect synaptic heterogeneity or cell type-specific features, which are crucial for understanding how variants differently affect synapse subtypes. <sentence_start/>For example, the G226R variant may particularly impact synapses involved in high-frequency neurotransmission, such as those of fast-spiking interneurons. <sentence_start/>These cell type-specific vulnerabilities can disrupt the delicate balance between excitation and inhibition. <sentence_start/>In addition, <italic toggle="yes">NGN2</italic>-induced neurons are known to exhibit substantial molecular and functional heterogeneity, generating diverse neuronal subtypes and maturation states depending on factors such as expression levels and differentiation conditions.<citation rid="bib61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.stemcr.2021.07.006" pmid="34358451" pmcid="PMC8452516" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This intrinsic variability may further influence the observed electrophysiological phenotypes and should be considered when interpreting network-level effects.

Another limitation of this study is the absence of direct causal validation linking the observed phenotypes to the <italic toggle="yes">STX1B</italic> variants, as rescue experiments through the generation of isogenic controls were not performed. <sentence_start/>While the use of patient-derived iPSCs provides a relevant genetic context, the contribution of genetic background effects cannot be fully excluded. <sentence_start/>Future studies incorporating isogenic rescue approaches could further strengthen the causal interpretation of the observed phenotypes.

Despite these considerations, our findings represent an important piece in dissecting SNARE-related pathologies in a human model representing the genetic constellation of affected individuals and underscore the need for future investigations using more sophisticated models to fully elucidate variant-specific effects on neuronal networks.
